title: India Orders Air India to Overhaul Drug Testing After Phuket Pilot's Marijuana Positive
excerpt: The aviation ministry has directed the DGCA to urgently revise its drug-testing framework and increase the share of personnel covered, following a pattern of substance-related incidents.
body:
• India's aviation ministry has directed the DGCA to urgently revise its drug-testing framework and expand the proportion of aviation personnel covered by mandatory screening.
  • The directive follows the August 4 Phuket-Delhi flight incident where the captain tested positive for marijuana after the aircraft dropped 300 feet mid-flight, injuring 17 people.
  • Under current rules, airlines must randomly test at least 10 percent of flight crew annually — far below the US standard of 25 percent.
  • Air India has faced three substance-related crew incidents in under a year, including a pilot deported from San Francisco with marijuana in April.

India's government has directed Air India to strengthen its operational safety oversight and ordered the Directorate General of Civil Aviation to urgently overhaul its drug-testing framework for aviation personnel, following the confirmed marijuana positive of an Air India captain whose Phuket-Delhi flight dropped 300 feet mid-cruise on August 4.

The Ministry of Civil Aviation has asked the DGCA to increase the proportion of pilots, cabin crew, and air traffic controllers covered by mandatory psychoactive substance testing, according to The Times of India. Officials signaled zero tolerance: "Guilty will not be spared."

The Incident That Forced Action

On August 4, Air India flight AI2379 — an Airbus A320neo carrying 137 passengers and eight crew — experienced a sudden altitude loss of approximately 300 feet while cruising over Odisha. The aircraft stabilized and landed safely in Delhi, but 13 passengers and four crew members sustained injuries. The Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau has classified the event as a "serious incident."

https://x.com/ShivAroor/status/2087235229694210163

Under standard procedures, both pilots underwent psychoactive substance screening after landing. The captain's initial test flagged a positive result, and a confirmatory laboratory test confirmed the presence of marijuana. Reports also indicate the captain was taking sleep medication at the time of the flight.

The Ministry summoned Air India CEO Campbell Wilson to explain the airline's safety protocols. The DGCA took both crew members off roster pending the investigation's outcome.

"The worldwide spread of use of psychoactive substances, their general availability and the ever-increasing number of addicted users is a serious concern to aviation safety."

— Directorate General of Civil Aviation, India

A Pattern of Incidents

The Phuket flight is not an isolated case. In April 2026, an Air India co-pilot was deported from San Francisco International Airport after US Customs and Border Protection found marijuana in his luggage. He had been deadheading to SFO to operate a return flight. In December 2025, Canadian authorities removed an Air India captain from command at Vancouver Airport after the pilot failed two breathalyzer tests.

These incidents have put Air India's safety culture under intense scrutiny at a time when the Tata Group-owned carrier is spending billions on fleet modernization and brand rehabilitation.

Current Testing Rules and Their Gaps

The DGCA's existing drug-testing framework, introduced in 2023, requires airlines and air navigation service providers to randomly test at least 10 percent of flight crew and air traffic controllers annually for eight categories of psychoactive substances, including cannabis, cocaine, amphetamines, opioids, and benzodiazepines.

A first positive test results in mandatory rehabilitation. A second leads to a three-year license suspension. A third means permanent cancellation. All positive cases must be reported to the DGCA within 24 hours.

By comparison, the US Federal Aviation Administration requires airlines to randomly test 25 percent of all safety-sensitive employees each year — two and a half times India's current threshold. The government's directive to increase India's testing coverage narrows that gap.

The DGCA also tightened alcohol-testing rules earlier this year, mandating video-recorded breath-analyzer tests for all crew with recordings preserved for six months, and imposing stricter penalties for violations.

What's Next

The DGCA is expected to issue revised Civil Aviation Requirements expanding the scope and frequency of drug testing. Whether the revised rules apply industry-wide or single out Air India remains to be seen, though the government's language — directing both the airline and the regulator — suggests broader reform.

For Air India, the stakes extend beyond regulatory compliance. The airline has staked its post-Tata revival on premium service and safety credentials. Repeated substance-related incidents involving its crew risk undermining that narrative just as retrofitted aircraft and new routes begin to change passenger perceptions.
